opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it was that it felt like the most interesting open problem in the field at that moment. Before joining OpenAI, I'd spent time on things like game-playing and strategic reasoning, and one lesson that stuck with me from that world was how much you gain when a system can actually *think* at test time: search, plan, consider alternatives, rather than just producing an answer in one shot.

By late 2023, language models had gotten remarkably good at a broad range of things, but on hard multi-step problems like tricky math, competition-style questions, and long chains of logic, they'd often confidently go off the rails. It felt like there was a clear gap between what these models knew and what they could do with that knowledge if you just gave them room to reason. So the question that grabbed me was: can we get models to spend more compute thinking, and have that thinking actually pay off in a reliable, scalable way?

There was also a sense of momentum internally. People were starting to see early signs that training models to reason, with reinforcement learning on problems where you can check whether the answer is right, led to real improvements, not just cosmetic ones. When you see a curve that keeps going up as you put in more thinking time, that's very exciting as a researcher. It suggested a new axis of scaling beyond just making models bigger.

And personally, I've always loved math and hard problems. The idea of building a system that could eventually tackle problems at the level of, say, olympiad mathematics, where you need creativity, rigor, and persistence, felt like a really meaningful milestone to aim for. So it was a mix of the scientific opportunity, the timing, and just genuine curiosity about whether we could get there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that models often went off track on hard multi-step problems and describes a gap between what they knew and what they could do, identifying that reasoning limitation as what drew him to the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it came from a bit of frustration mixed with curiosity. I'd spent a lot of time around competition math, and I had this very concrete sense of what it feels like to actually reason through a hard problem: you try something, it fails, you back up, you notice a structure you missed. And when I looked at the models at the time, they were remarkable at a lot of things, but they didn't do that. They'd produce a confident, fluent answer in one pass, and if the first step was wrong, the whole thing was wrong, and the model had no mechanism to catch it.

So the question that really pulled me in was: what if we let the model think before it answers? Not just prompt it to show its work, but actually train it so that spending more compute at inference time, exploring and checking and revising, reliably translates into better answers. That felt like a genuinely different axis of scaling than just making the pretraining run bigger. And in late 2023 there were early signs internally that this axis was real, that the curves went up when you gave the model room to reason. Once you see a curve like that, it's very hard to work on anything else.

The other piece was that math and code gave us a place to measure it honestly. You can't fool a verifier. Either the proof holds or it doesn't, either the tests pass or they don't. That made it a clean place to develop the ideas, with the hope that whatever we learned about reasoning there would carry over to messier domains. That hope was a big part of the draw.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the models at the time did not reason through hard problems, instead answering in one pass without catching a wrong first step, and identifies this gap as what drew Wei to the work.

astra-6.text:
What drew me in was the idea that a model could do more if you gave it room to think. With a difficult math or coding problem, you don’t necessarily know the answer immediately—you try something, check it, and revise. I was interested in whether we could train models to make productive use of that same process.

There was a very compelling research question there: could we improve a model’s answers by teaching it how to work through a problem, and then giving it more time to do that? That felt like a direction worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes interest in giving models more room and time to reason, but does not identify existing models’ conspicuous inability to reason as the initial draw.

sol-6.1.text: What drew me in was the idea that a model could do better by spending more time thinking about a problem. With a hard math or coding problem, you don’t necessarily expect a person to get the answer immediately. You give them time to explore an approach, notice a mistake, and try something else. I was interested in whether we could train models to use that time productively, too. That felt like a compelling research direction: improving not just what a model knows, but its ability to work through something difficult.

r001.rationale: The response says models might improve by spending more time thinking and working through difficult problems. It does not identify existing models’ conspicuous inability to reason as what initially drew Wei to the work.
